name: Nitrux
summary: 64-bit Linux distribution built on Debian, characterised by an immutable root through OverlayFS, the OpenRC init system, the Hyprland Wayland compositor and the rootless NX AppHub software management.
license: GNU GPLv3 and associated free licences

content.introduction: Nitrux is a Linux distribution for personal computers developed by Nitrux Latinoamericana S.C. under the direction of Uri Herrera. Initially designed around Ubuntu and KDE components, it has undergone several major architectural changes to become a stand-alone desktop operating system based on Debian, using the OpenRC init system and an immutable system root managed by OverlayFS. It favours a modern Wayland display stack animated by the dynamic tiling compositor Hyprland, applications built on the MauiKit toolkit and a distribution of user applications without administrator privileges relying on NX AppHub and the AppImage format.
content.what_is_it: It is a desktop operating system integrating a system immutability model coupled with containerised and encapsulated application management. Nitrux isolates its root file system in read-only mode in order to guarantee the consistency of the base system and to avoid alterations caused by direct package installations. Graphical and utility applications are supplied through formats decoupled from the base system (AppBoxes, Flatpak, Distrobox), while the central components receive atomic OTA (Over-The-Air) updates orchestrated by the NUTS (Nitrux Update Tool System) system tool.
content.immutable_architecture_and_overlayroot: Since version 2.6.0 (January 2023), Nitrux applies a strict immutability policy to the root file system through its NX Overlayroot module. Relying on OverlayFS, the system root is mounted read-only during normal startup. Direct modifications of the system hierarchy (`/usr`, `/bin`, `/lib`) are blocked by default, which protects the system against accidental corruption and malicious software. Only the user data directory (`/home`) and the persistent state paths (`/var/lib`) keep permanent write rights. This separation makes it possible to ensure reproducible atomic backups and restorations during operating system version upgrades.
content.openrc_and_debian_base: Unlike the majority of contemporary Debian or Ubuntu-based Linux distributions, Nitrux has set aside the systemd service manager in favour of OpenRC for its init system. OpenRC manages the startup of system daemons, the configuration of runlevels and the management of background services with a reduced memory footprint and a clear separation between initialisation and user process management. The software base is built directly from the Debian package branches, adapted by the development team with Linux kernels configured for high interactive performance (including zstd level 6 compression and processor latency optimisations).
content.nx_apphub_and_appboxes: Nitrux adopts an application management paradigm without root rights (*rootless*). The traditional APT package manager is disabled for the direct installation of application software on the host so as not to compromise the integrity of the root. As a replacement, Nitrux provides NX AppHub, a command-line tool and integration daemon that declaratively assembles Debian packages into self-contained packages called AppBoxes. AppBoxes rely on the FUSE 3 runtime and the AppImage format, integrating their dependencies and running the software under the control of sandbox profiles (Bubblewrap, Firejail or AppArmor). For development needs or software unavailable in this form, the system supports Flatpak at user level as well as Distrobox for running containers of other Linux distributions.
content.hyprland_and_mauikit_desktop: Nitrux's graphical environment is articulated around the Hyprland Wayland compositor, configured to offer fluid and responsive tiling window navigation. The desktop's native applications rely on MauiKit, a modular graphical interface framework developed by the project (supplied in the form of a specific fork adapted to Linux). This set provides a collection of consistent tools (Index file manager, station terminal, VVave multimedia player) suited to modern screen resolutions and to touch or keyboard interactions. The system verifies hardware compatibility during the boot phase through the HCVL (*Hardware Compatibility Validation Layer*) software layer and supplies separate ISO images optimised for AMD/Intel or NVIDIA GPUs.
content.system_requirements: The official documentation sets a minimum of 4 GB of RAM, an x86 64-bit processor compatible with AVX2 (x86-64-v3 level), 64 GB of storage and 512 MB of video memory. The firmware must be EFI or UEFI: machines with legacy BIOS are not supported, and CSM booting is only conditional. An Internet connection is optional during installation but necessary for updates. The project notes that a system can boot with 2 GB of memory, but that this use remains limited to light tasks.
content.gpu_support_limits: Graphics cards must provide Mesa GBM/KMS support, or, for NVIDIA, a working open-source kernel module. The documentation explicitly excludes NVIDIA GPUs that depend on the Nouveau driver or on the proprietary driver, ATI/AMD GCN 1.0 and earlier cards, and obsolete GPUs. These restrictions follow from the choice of Wayland and Hyprland as the default graphical environment.
content.init_system_rationale: Nitrux uses OpenRC instead of systemd. The documentation justifies this choice by the Unix philosophy: OpenRC is described as a process launcher that relies on the init supplied by the system, ensures process isolation, parallel startup and service dependency management, without absorbing ancillary functions. systemd is presented there as a software suite encompassing device manager, session manager, network manager and logging service.
content.installation_workflow: The installation guide distinguishes an ISO image for AMD and Intel hardware and a separate image for NVIDIA, then describes the validation of the integrity and authenticity of the image, writing to a USB key with Rufus, Ventoy or dd, and the installation process. Partitioning can be automated or manual; disk encryption, enabling Secure Boot, installation in single or dual boot with Windows or another Linux distribution, and triple booting are documented separately.
content.recommended_configuration: The configuration recommended by the documentation is 8 GB of RAM, an x86 64-bit processor of x86-64-v3 level with AVX2, an 8th generation Intel processor (Coffee Lake) or an AMD Ryzen 1000 or more recent, USB 3.0 booting and NVMe storage. Virtualisation extensions and IOMMU are cited among the capabilities expected from the firmware. EFI or UEFI firmware remains necessary, Secure Boot remaining optional.
content.release_history_and_version_series: The release archive lists the successive versions with their publication announcements: 7.0.0, 6.1.0, 6.0.0, 5.1.0 and 5.0.0, preceded by a series carrying short codenames - 3.9.1 "mk", 3.9.0 "pd", 3.8.0 "db", 3.7.1 "sp" and 3.7.0 "ub". The home page designates 7.0.0 as the latest release, and the site footer dates the project's activity from 2017 to 2026 under Nitrux Latinoamericana S.C. Each entry in the archive links both a changelog and the announcement published for that version, so the version history is documented release by release rather than summarised in a single page.
content.secure_boot_encryption_and_image_validat: The documentation devotes a specific chapter set to integrity and boot: it distinguishes the ISO built for AMD and Intel hardware from the one built for NVIDIA hardware, documents an integrity validation step and a separate authenticity validation step for the downloaded image, and describes flashing with USB Flash Preflight, Rufus, Ventoy or dd. Installation is documented with automated and non-automated partitioning options, full-disk encryption, and single-boot, dual-boot and triple-boot scenarios, including a dedicated page on using Secure Boot with Nitrux.
advantages: Immutable system root through NX Overlayroot and OverlayFS guaranteeing the integrity of the base system against corruption and package conflicts.
Atomic operating system updates orchestrated by NUTS without risk of state breakage midway.
Rootless software management through NX AppHub (AppBoxes), Flatpak and Distrobox preserving the stability of the host system.
OpenRC init system offering a lightweight and modular alternative to the systemd architecture.
Modern graphical environment articulated around the Hyprland Wayland compositor and the MauiKit application suite.
Linux kernels optimised for low latency and hardware integration validated from boot through HCVL.
disadvantages: Incompatibility with the traditional habits of Debian administration (impossibility of using `apt install` directly on the root in normal mode).
Demanding learning curve for users not familiar with Wayland tiling compositors and environments without systemd.
Strict hardware requirements limited to modern x86_64 architectures with UEFI firmware.
Increased disk space consumption linked to the duplication of dependencies in self-contained package formats and containers.
who_is_it_for: Advanced users looking for a contemporary Wayland desktop work environment with tiling management.
Developers and technicians wishing for an immutable workstation with isolated dependency management through containers and AppBoxes.
Linux enthusiasts wishing to use a Debian-based distribution articulated around OpenRC rather than systemd.
who_is_it_not_for: Linux beginners accustomed to traditional desktop paradigms (classic floating menus, direct package installation through APT).
Users of old computers or computers limited in RAM and disk space not meeting the minimum hardware specifications.
System administrators whose software infrastructure depends strictly on systemd daemons and service units.
content.verdict: Nitrux constitutes a singular and resolutely technical proposal in the landscape of Linux distributions. By combining a Debian base stripped of systemd in favour of OpenRC, an immutable root protected by OverlayFS, a Wayland desktop articulated around Hyprland and containerised and declarative application management, the project addresses experienced users who favour architectural resilience and modern operational efficiency.

components.name: Debian
components.note: Base distribution: "Nitrux is a 64-bit-only Linux desktop distribution built from Debian."; the same page adds that Nitrux is "up to date, thanks to recent Debian releases and the performance-oriented kernel configurations we chose" (nxos.org/home/nx).

components.name: OpenRC
components.note: "Nitrux also does not use systemd as its init system; instead, it uses OpenRC, a simpler init and service manager." (nxos.org/home/nx).

components.name: Hyprland
components.note: "It uses the Hyprland window compositor and our bespoke Wayland-focused Workspace Environment." (nxos.org/home/nx).
